title: Which Attention Heads Copy the Harmful Context? Tracing Information Flow in Jailbroken Completions

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: identifying the specific 'harm-copy' attention heads that fail during jailbreaks provides a low-level mechanistic target for hardening via amplification, failure-mode characterization, or adversarial training on those specific heads.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Comparing attention patterns between refused and jailbroken prompts using TransformerLens, plus attention knockout experiments, is intermediate complexity. Well-documented tooling exists, though composing the full pipeline requires guidance.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: identify the minimal set of heads whose knockout reproduces the jailbreak effect. Clear experimental protocol comparing two prompt conditions with a measurable outcome (refusal direction drop).

novelty.reasoning: This idea is substantially covered by existing work. 'On the Role of Attention Heads in Large Language Model Safety' (ICLR 2025) identifies attention heads that influence harmful vs safe responses by comparing activation patterns between rejected and jailbroken prompts, and uses interpolation of internal representations to suppress harmful outputs. 'Jailbreak Defense in LLM via Attention Head Analysis and Selective Intervention' directly addresses selective intervention on identified heads. 'Attention Slipping: A Mechanistic Understanding of Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses in LLMs' (2025) provides mechanistic understanding of attention shifts during jailbreaks. The proposed contribution of identifying 'harm-copy' heads and performing knockout experiments is largely subsumed by these papers.
